about:
Phish-Tac-Toe

Three boards, nine songs each. A square lights up when Phish plays that song tonight. First to three in a row — across, down or diagonal — wins. If more than one board completes a line, the winner is whoever's line finished earlier in the show, which the app works out from the actual setlist order.

Why these 25 songs

Every setlist Phish played in 1996 (71 shows) and every show since Jan 2023 (165 shows) was pulled from the Phantasy Tour API. Each candidate got two numbers: how core it was to 1996, and how often the band still plays it. The score blends them, weighted 0.4 / 0.8 — meaning current rotation actually matters a bit more than era authenticity.

Everything already played is gone

Phish doesn't repeat inside a run, and this is night five: the first four nights (1992, 1993, 1994, 1995) burned 86 songs, including almost the entire 1996 core — Divided Sky, Runaway Jim, Split Open and Melt, Stash, Simple, Down with Disease, Taste, Theme, Free, Sample. Tonight is played from what's left, which makes the leftovers weirdly predictable: the model is more confident about tonight than about any other night of the run.

Does the model actually work?

It was backtested against this run's first three nights — scoring each night with that year's own play rates, and excluding whatever the earlier nights had used. It put about half of each night's real setlist in its top picks, against roughly 17% for guessing at random. The percentages on the squares are calibrated: squares marked 30% hit about 30% of the time in that test.

The center square

Character Zero is the center of all three boards on purpose. It's the single likeliest song left — the Billy Breathes rocker that 1996 minted as a set-closer, and they've played it 94% of the nights of this run's era. When it drops, all three boards light up together and nobody gets an edge from the one near-certainty. (You Enjoy Myself, the model's white whale, is finally down to one board — it flagged YEM as a top pick on every night of this run and has been wrong all four times.)

Fairness

The other 24 were placed by an optimizer that simulated 8,000 possible versions of tonight and balanced the thing that actually matters — who wins the game, not just who gets a line. Checked against 60,000 further simulated shows on a separate random generator:

boardwinsgets a lineavg score
Rob31.4%57.8%4.51
Justin31.2%61.5%4.47
Jayme30.3%62.1%4.50

Somebody wins about 93% of the time.

The one square the model didn't pick

Hello My Baby is on here by choice, not by score. The 1903 barbershop number was 1996's running gag — the band sang it a cappella at 17 of the year's 71 shows, including the Clifford Ball. It hasn't been in rotation for years (zero shows since Jan 2023), which is exactly why its square says 24% and not something flattering. The other story square earned its spot honestly: Crosseyed and Painless, from the Remain in Light Halloween costume, is back in heavy rotation and rates 50% on the numbers alone.

If the feed lags

The setlist feed is re-checked about every 30 seconds during the show. If it falls behind, hit Manual entry and mark squares yourself — those marks stay on your own phone and can only add hits, never remove one.

Odds are one model's opinion, not gospel. Phish will do whatever Phish wants. That's the entire point.

A Day in the Life.title: A Day in the Life
A Day in the Life.bio: The Beatles classic from Sgt. Pepper's (1967). Page sings John's dreamy verses, Trey takes Paul's "woke up, fell out of bed" bit, and the band builds that giant crashing orchestra swell all by itself.
A Day in the Life.lyric: I read the news today oh boy
A Day in the Life.why: The Beatles habit carried straight into 1996: 15 of the year's 71 shows, from the April Jazz Fest date through the December run.
A Day in the Life.fact: It was played deep into night two of the Clifford Ball on 8/17/96, right before Possum — the giant orchestral swell over a decommissioned Air Force base.

Buried Alive.title: Buried Alive
Buried Alive.bio: A short, frantic Phish instrumental — zero lyrics, just Trey shredding. The panicked pace is meant to sound like someone clawing their way out of a grave, which makes it a killer set-opener.
Buried Alive.why: Nearly extinct in 1996 — just 2 plays all year — but the modern band loves it again (12 shows since 2023), and that current-rotation weight is what earns its square.
Buried Alive.fact: One of its two 1996 outings was 10/16/96 at the Olympic Center in Lake Placid — the arena built for the 1980 'Miracle on Ice' Olympic hockey final.

Cars Trucks Buses.title: Cars Trucks Buses
Cars Trucks Buses.bio: A short, bouncy instrumental written by Page — named after the rest-stop sign — built around his clavinet. No lyrics at all, just a tight two-minute keyboard workout, usually in the first set.
Cars Trucks Buses.why: 1996 put it on the map: 19 of the year's 71 shows, plus track five on Billy Breathes, released that October. The band barely touches it now, which is exactly what makes it a theme-night special.
Cars Trucks Buses.fact: Played early on night two of the Clifford Ball and again in the first set of the 12/31/96 New Year's show in Boston — Page's little rest-stop tune had a very good year.

Character Zero.title: Character Zero
Character Zero.bio: The Billy Breathes rocker that 1996 minted: a big, blunt, riff-driven anthem that closes sets, with Trey wailing over one of the band's simplest and most effective grooves. Loosely inspired by the Kurt Vonnegut line about being what you pretend to be.
Character Zero.lyric: I was taught a month ago to bide my time and take it slow
Character Zero.why: The definitive 1996 song — it debuted that June, appeared at 21 of the year's 71 shows, and it's still the band's go-to closer: 31 shows since 2023 make it the single likeliest song left unburned.
Character Zero.fact: It debuted at a tiny club warm-up gig at the Joyous Lake in Woodstock before the band left to tour Europe with Santana, then bookended the year: played at the Remain in Light Halloween show and again on 12/31/96 in Boston.

Crosseyed and Painless.title: Crosseyed and Painless
Crosseyed and Painless.bio: A Talking Heads song from Remain in Light (1980), the album Phish performed start to finish as their 1996 Halloween costume. The nervous funk groove fit the band so well that the cover outlived the costume and became a jam vehicle in its own right.
Crosseyed and Painless.lyric: Lost my shape, trying to act casual
Crosseyed and Painless.why: THE 1996 story song: the Remain in Light costume is the single most famous thing Phish did that year, and unlike most costume tracks this one earned a permanent place — 15 shows since 2023. Its square needs no charity.
Crosseyed and Painless.fact: Santana's percussionist Karl Perazzo sat in for the whole Halloween set. The song's "still waiting…" refrain became a permanent piece of Phish vocabulary, teased inside other jams for the next thirty years.

Esther.title: Esther
Esther.bio: A dark storybook epic from Junta about a girl given an enchanted marionette at a traveling circus, and the mob that chases her to a grim watery ending. Composed, creepy, and almost never played.
Esther.lyric: It was late one fall night at a fairground near town
Esther.why: Only three shows in 1996 — but one of them was the Clifford Ball, and the modern band has revived it (6 shows since 2023), so the puppet is officially back.
Esther.fact: Esther at the Clifford Ball, 8/16/96: a ten-minute gothic fairy tale for 70,000 people at an Air Force base, fifth song of the festival.

Fee.title: Fee
Fee.bio: Trey's storybook original from Junta about Fee the Buddhist weasel, a singer named Millie Grace, and Floyd the villainous chimpanzee. The tell is the megaphone: Trey sings the verses through it for a tinny, far-off sound.
Fee.why: Ten shows in 1996, from the Joyous Lake warm-up in June through the fall tour — a steady deep-cut presence all year.
Fee.fact: Played on night two of the Clifford Ball, megaphone and all, in front of the biggest audience the song has ever had.

Fire.title: Fire
Fire.bio: The Jimi Hendrix Experience classic, played fast and unhinged — Fishman's double-time drumming chasing Trey's solo. A show-closer by design: three minutes of gasoline.
Fire.lyric: Let me stand next to your fire
Fire.why: Eight 1996 shows, and it's back in the modern deck too — the exact profile of a one-song encore on a theme night.
Fire.fact: It CLOSED the 6/6/96 Joyous Lake warm-up — the tiny Woodstock club gig that launched the whole 1996 campaign — and kept turning up through the fall.

Frankenstein.title: Frankenstein
Frankenstein.bio: The Edgar Winter Group's 1973 #1 instrumental, all monster riff and synth freakout. It's the one song where Page straps on the keytar and comes out from behind the rig to duel Trey at the front of the stage.
Frankenstein.why: Eight 1996 shows — it entered the repertoire's front line that August and hung around all fall, and the keytar still comes out most tours.
Frankenstein.fact: Played on night two of the Clifford Ball on 8/17/96, deep in the day's final set — Page, a keytar, and 70,000 people.

Ginseng Sullivan.title: Ginseng Sullivan
Ginseng Sullivan.bio: A Norman Blake bluegrass tune about a Mississippi ginseng digger dreaming of getting back home to the delta. Mike sings it; the band has treated it as their acoustic-flavored breather since 1993.
Ginseng Sullivan.lyric: It's a long way from the delta to the north Georgia mountains
Ginseng Sullivan.why: Six shows in the fall of 1996 alone — it came roaring back on the October leg and stayed through the New Year's run.
Ginseng Sullivan.fact: All six 1996 versions came after 10/21 — it was purely a fall-tour toy that year, capped by a 12/28/96 appearance in the Boston year-end run.

Guyute.title: Guyute
Guyute.bio: A four-movement mini-symphony about an ugly pig who dances a jig, pulls weapons from his coat, and lectures the narrator in a strange language. Trey wrote it alongside My Friend My Friend while in Ireland.
Guyute.debut: 1994-10-07, Stabler Arena, Lehigh University, Bethlehem PA
Guyute.why: Six shows in 1996, starting on the European summer tour, as the band kept polishing its knottiest composition on the road.
Guyute.fact: Its last 1996 outing was 12/30/96 in Boston, the night before New Year's — a ten-minute composed epic dropped into an arena run.

Hello My Baby.title: Hello My Baby
Hello My Baby.bio: The 1899 Tin Pan Alley number — yes, the singing-frog song from the Looney Tunes cartoon — arranged for four-part barbershop harmony. The band gathers around one mic, no instruments, and hams it up.
Hello My Baby.lyric: Hello my baby, hello my honey, hello my ragtime gal
Hello My Baby.why: This is the story square: 17 of 1996's 71 shows sang it, including the Clifford Ball — it was that year's running a cappella gag. It hasn't been in rotation for years, and the square honestly says so.
Hello My Baby.fact: Sung at the Clifford Ball on 8/16/96: four guys, one microphone, an 1899 barbershop tune, and the largest rock audience in North America that year.

Horn.title: Horn
Horn.bio: A short, chiming Trey original from Rift — a single bright guitar line over a lilting groove, in and out in four minutes. One of the prettiest small songs in the catalogue, with no jam and no ambitions beyond the melody.
Horn.why: A four-play rarity in 1996 that the current band has picked back up (6 shows since 2023) — exactly the kind of small song a theme night makes room for.
Horn.fact: Its 1996 return came 7/12/96 at the Melkweg, the legendary ~1,500-capacity Amsterdam club, during the strangest tour Phish ever did.

I Didn't Know.title: I Didn't Know
I Didn't Know.bio: A goofy barbershop-flavored singalong from the earliest days of the band, and the classic excuse to introduce Fishman on vacuum cleaner: Trey presents "the Greasy Fizeek," Fish steps out from the kit, and solos into a running Electrolux.
I Didn't Know.why: Six 1996 shows, starting 7/11/96 at London's Shepherd's Bush Empire — and it's back in the modern rotation whenever Fishman needs a vacuum feature.
I Didn't Know.fact: Every version is really a Fishman delivery mechanism: in 1996 it meant vacuum solos for European club crowds who had no idea what they were looking at.

If I Could.title: If I Could
If I Could.bio: The prettiest thing on Hoist — a slow, aching Trey/Tom Marshall ballad that the band almost never plays. Alison Krauss sang harmony on the studio version.
If I Could.why: Just two 1996 performances — but one was Red Rocks — and the modern band has quietly brought it back (5 shows since 2023), which is what lifts a two-play rarity onto a board.
If I Could.fact: Both 1996 versions came on the Santana summer: 7/21/96 in Europe and 8/5/96 at Red Rocks, and then it vanished again for years.

Lawn Boy.title: Lawn Boy
Lawn Boy.bio: The title track of the 1990 album and Page's lounge-lizard showcase: he steps out front and croons it like a Vegas act while the band vamps cocktail jazz behind him, then hands it back with a flourish.
Lawn Boy.why: Four shows in 1996 — including the infamous Red Rocks stand — and still a semi-regular treat today, so the crooner odds are real.
Lawn Boy.fact: Played 8/7/96 on the final night of the Red Rocks residency — the last night of Phish the town of Morrison, Colorado ever allowed.

McGrupp and the Watchful Hosemasters.title: McGrupp and the Watchful Hosemasters
McGrupp and the Watchful Hosemasters.bio: An ancient Phish original built from a Tom Marshall poem — McGrupp is Colonel Forbin's dog in the Gamehendge story. After the weird lyrics it opens into an instrumental suite and a long Page piano solo.
McGrupp and the Watchful Hosemasters.lyric: But he looks too much like… Dave
McGrupp and the Watchful Hosemasters.why: A four-play rarity in 1996 that the modern band has quietly revived — 8 shows since 2023 — which is the profile of a sneaky theme-night pick.
McGrupp and the Watchful Hosemasters.fact: Its 1996 return came 7/23/96 at the Markthalle in Hamburg, on the strange summer tour where Phish played European clubs and festivals while opening stadium dates for Santana.

Old Home Place.title: Old Home Place
Old Home Place.bio: A bluegrass standard written by The Dillards' Mitch Jayne and Dean Webb and made famous by J.D. Crowe — a man trades the family homestead for a girl and a job, and loses all three. Phish plays it straight, harmonies and all.
Old Home Place.lyric: It's been ten long years since I left my home
Old Home Place.why: Five shows in 1996, and the modern band still reaches for it (6 since 2023) whenever they want two minutes of real bluegrass.
Old Home Place.fact: It OPENED night two of the Clifford Ball on 8/17/96 — seventy thousand people, and Phish walks out and starts with a Dillards bluegrass number.

Poor Heart.title: Poor Heart
Poor Heart.bio: A Mike Gordon original from A Picture of Nectar, written after someone stole his four-track tape recorder. It's a breakneck two-minute bluegrass burner that Mike sings at full speed.
Poor Heart.lyric: You won't steal my poor heart again
Poor Heart.why: One of the most-played songs of 1996 at 21 of 71 shows — the band's favorite way to reset a set with two minutes of bluegrass panic.
Poor Heart.fact: It was the second song of the 6/6/96 Joyous Lake club gig that opened the year's touring — the little Woodstock bar show where Character Zero and Waste debuted.

Rocky Top.title: Rocky Top
Rocky Top.bio: The Osborne Brothers' bluegrass standard (and one of Tennessee's official state songs), written by Boudleaux and Felice Bryant in ten minutes in 1967. Phish rips through it in two minutes flat.
Rocky Top.lyric: Good ol' Rocky Top, Rocky Top Tennessee
Rocky Top.why: Seven 1996 shows, from the Hamburg Markthalle in July to the December arenas — the band's default encore-sized bluegrass blast that year.
Rocky Top.fact: 1996 took Rocky Top to Europe: its first outing of the year was 7/23/96 in a Hamburg market hall, about as far from Tennessee as the song has ever been.

The Mango Song.title: The Mango Song
The Mango Song.bio: A Lawn Boy-era oddity with one of the great absurdist Phish lyrics — hands and feet turning into mangos, newspapers, genius. Tricky interlocking parts disguised as a breezy island tune.
The Mango Song.lyric: Your hands and feet are mangos, you're gonna be a genius anyway
The Mango Song.why: Four 1996 shows, and its comeback that August happened at Red Rocks — plus 5 shows since 2023 keeps it plausibly in the deck tonight.
The Mango Song.fact: Its 1996 return came 8/4/96 at Red Rocks, the first night of a four-show stand so oversold and chaotic that the town of Morrison never let Phish back.

Train Song.title: Train Song
Train Song.bio: A quiet Mike Gordon ballad from Billy Breathes, barely two minutes long, written with Vermont songwriter Robert Linitz. Three-part harmony over a gentle sway — the kind of breather the band drops between monsters.
Train Song.why: A genuine 1996 baby: it debuted that July in Europe and racked up 15 of the year's 71 shows as the band worked the Billy Breathes material in.
Train Song.fact: Played at the Clifford Ball on 8/16/96, two months before Billy Breathes came out — the crowd of 70,000 was hearing an unreleased song.

Waste.title: Waste
Waste.bio: The gentlest song on Billy Breathes — a quiet Trey/Tom Marshall love song that the arena sings back word for word. It floats where most Phish songs churn, and it's become a beloved encore and jam-landing pad.
Waste.lyric: Come waste your time with me
Waste.why: Born in 1996: it debuted at the June club warm-up, appeared at 17 of the year's 71 shows, and unlike most of that list it never left the rotation.
Waste.fact: Played mid-set at the Clifford Ball in front of ~70,000 people — the biggest rock concert in North America that year — three months before Billy Breathes was even released.

Ya Mar.title: Ya Mar
Ya Mar.bio: A calypso cover by Bahamian musician Cyril Ferguson, sung by Mike, and one of Phish's bounciest dance tunes. Trey hollers "Play it, Leo!" to hand Page a piano solo — which is where Page's nickname came from.
Ya Mar.why: A 1996 workhorse at 19 of 71 shows, from the New Orleans Jazz Fest date in April to the year-end run, and still a live regular today.
Ya Mar.fact: It was the third song of the first Clifford Ball set on 8/16/96 — sunshine, 70,000 people, and a calypso tune from a Bahamian bar band's repertoire.

You Enjoy Myself.title: You Enjoy Myself
You Enjoy Myself.bio: Trey wrote it in 1985 while busking through Europe, and it's now the most-played song Phish has. Twenty-odd minutes: a long composed section, Trey and Mike bouncing in sync on trampolines, a Mike bass solo, then a wordless vocal jam.
You Enjoy Myself.why: Played at 23 of 1996's 71 shows — including Halloween — and the model's white whale: it flagged YEM as a top pick on all four previous nights of this run and has been wrong every single time. If they're ever playing it, it's tonight.
You Enjoy Myself.fact: On 10/31/96 in Atlanta it anchored the first set of the Remain in Light Halloween show. Tonight is the last chance of the run — after this there is no more saving it.
